The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (the Alliance) subversion case will deliver its verdict on 21 August. Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung, who pleaded not guilty, have been remanded in custody for nearly five years due to this case. In the case, the Alliance's slogan "End one-party dictatorship," chanted for over 30 years, was accused by the prosecution as equivalent to "ending Communist Party leadership" and subverting or destroying the fundamental system of the state, constituting incitement to subvert state power through "illegal means." However, the defence rebutted that "End one-party dictatorship" merely calls for ending the illegitimate "party dictatorship" and building a democratic China, and does not equate to ending Communist Party leadership. The defendants bear no hostility towards the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) and have no intent to subvert. The prosecution also failed to specify what actions the Alliance encouraged people to take to "End one-party dictatorship." What exactly are the prosecution's allegations? How did the defence rebut them? How did the court handle disputes over issues such as the Chinese Constitution and the June 4th incident? On the eve of the verdict, "集誌社" (FactWire) compiled nine key points and disputes from the 24-day trial. Related reports on the Alliance case

The Alliance, its chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, vice chairs Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung have been charged with incitement to subvert state power. The verdict will be delivered on 21 August.

控方的檢控基礎是什麼？

The Alliance, Lee Cheuk-yan, Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung have been charged with "incitement to subvert state power," accused of inciting others in Hong Kong to commit acts "aimed at subverting state power" through "illegal means"—that is, to overthrow or destroy the fundamental system of China as established by the Chinese Constitution, or to overthrow the central authorities. Among these, the prosecution defined "illegal means" as "ending the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party, in violation of the Chinese Constitution (in particular Article 1 and the Preamble)," treating so-called "violations of the Chinese Constitution" as "illegal."

The core of the charge lies in "End one-party dictatorship," one of the Alliance's five major objectives. The prosecution claimed that the Alliance, under the guise of "so-called democracy or the June 4th incident," combined with negative content targeting the state, advocated and promoted the "End one-party dictatorship" stance. Although there was no explicit or detailed plan, the "natural and reasonable effect" of this stance was to "end the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party."

The core of the prosecution's charge lies in "End one-party dictatorship," one of the Alliance's five major objectives, which the prosecution claims is equivalent to ending Communist Party leadership.

The prosecution's logic is that Article 1 of the Chinese Constitution, revised in 2018, stipulates: "The socialist system is the fundamental system of the People's Republic of China. The leadership of the Communist Party of China is the defining feature of Chinese socialism. No organization or individual may be allowed to undermine the socialist system." This reflects that CCP leadership is "the fundamental system of the state as established by the Constitution," and there is "no legal means" to end it. Therefore, the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" necessarily constitutes incitement to subvert state power through "illegal means" in violation of the Chinese Constitution.

However, this prosecution basis was rejected by the court during the mid-trial submissions. The judge considered the issue significant and far-reaching, but found the prosecution's submissions "superficial," lacking sufficient analysis or legal scholarship, and with no expert witnesses called. The court would not consider it. The court would only consider the prosecution's second basis: even if there were legal means to end CCP leadership, the Alliance was in effect not advocating constitutional amendment, but inciting people to use unlawful means to overthrow the Communist Party's leading position.

法庭應如何詮釋中國憲法？

As the charges involve the Chinese Constitution, how the court should understand and apply the relevant provisions became crucial. No Chinese constitutional experts were called to testify in this case. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the power to interpret the Constitution lies with the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, and Hong Kong courts have no jurisdiction to interpret it. Moreover, Hong Kong lawyers and judges are trained in common law and lack relevant knowledge. Without expert evidence and with no consensus between prosecution and defence, the court should not even interpret the constitutional provisions literally.

The prosecution agreed that Hong Kong courts have no power to interpret the Constitution, but argued that the wording is very clear and can be understood and applied literally without expert evidence. Lee Cheuk-yan's side also believed the court could interpret it literally, but if the prosecution made submissions beyond the literal meaning, expert evidence would be required; otherwise, such submissions should not be admitted.

The judge ultimately ruled that for constitutional provisions directly applicable to Hong Kong and relevant to the case—including the Preamble and Article 1 relied upon by the prosecution—the court could understand their plain meaning literally and in context as the basis for its decision, but could not rely on meanings beyond the literal text.

The charges involve the Chinese Constitution, and the prosecution did not call any experts. The judge ruled that the plain meaning could be understood literally and in context.

如何處理六四等政治議題？是非曲直是否相關？

The Alliance has been charged, and political issues such as June 4th inevitably entered the courtroom. In its opening statement, the prosecution stated that this is not a political trial and does not involve adjudicating any issues concerning democracy, June 4th, criticism of the state, history, or the merits of political systems. Whether the state Constitution aligns with democracy as the defendants claim, or the negative content they allege, "is fundamentally irrelevant to the case and need not be addressed by the court."

However, the prosecution also alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs to incite, using negative content to arouse hatred toward the regime to strengthen the inciting effect, and used June 4th vigils and the June 4th Memorial Museum to promote "End one-party dictatorship." The judge at one point quipped that the prosecution was saying the Alliance was "selling dog meat under the guise of selling mutton," but the prosecution denied this, stating, "We did not say what they said was false," and "it could be true," emphasizing that the point was exploiting related events to generate hatred of the CCP to achieve the goal of overthrowing Communist Party leadership.

The prosecution alleged that the defendants exploited current affairs to incite, and used the "June 4th Memorial Museum" and similar means to promote their stance.

The prosecution's claims were denied by the defence. Lee Cheuk-yan said the Alliance's actions were all protests in response to specific events—such as Liu Xiaobo's imprisonment, Liu Xia's house arrest, the 709 mass crackdown, and the alleged suicide of Li Wangyang—not smears under the guise of democracy. Chow Hang-tung emphasized that June 4th was a real event, not fabricated or used to smear the government. The focus of the June 4th vigil was mourning, and the Memorial Museum was for preserving and disseminating the truth. Accusing it of being established to promote an agenda puts the cart before the horse: "June 4th has never been a tool we used to incite 'End one-party dictatorship'... It is about lives, about blood, about crimes the government must face. It is not a tool to be exploited."

When Chow Hang-tung called witnesses to testify about what happened on June 4th, the judge interrupted and stopped her repeatedly, emphasizing that the court would not judge the rights and wrongs of June 4th. Chow rebutted that the prosecution accused the defendants of smearing and fabricating lies, so basic facts were needed to determine whether the allegations were true. If it could be established that the Alliance spoke the truth and made demands based on evidence, that would fall within the scope of freedom of speech. However, the judge reiterated that the court had no way of judging whether it was true, emphasizing that this case was not about June 4th, but about whether the National Security Law had been violated: "I will not let you use this opportunity for political propaganda."

Politics cannot be discussed, yet the prosecution used political reasoning to infer the defendants' intent. Lee Cheuk-yan's side noted in its closing that if the court does not address the relevant issues and cannot judge whether the criticism was justified, it should not conclude that the defendants exploited these issues to smear or cause hatred of the CCP.

Chow Hang-tung emphasized that June 4th was a real event, stating that it "is about lives, about blood," and is not a tool to be exploited.

「結束一黨專政」等於「結束共產黨領導」？等於「推翻、破壞國家根本制度」？

The core of the prosecution's charge is essentially a chain of equations: "End one-party dictatorship" = "End CCP leadership" = "Overthrow or destroy the fundamental system of the state." The defendants admitted to upholding "End one-party dictatorship," but denied that it equals "End CCP leadership."

Lee Cheuk-yan explained that the Alliance hoped to end dictatorship, not CCP leadership, and that dictatorship and democracy are opposites. "End one-party dictatorship" means hoping that people would enjoy basic rights and build a civil society, providing a basis for discussing democracy, and letting the people decide whether the Communist Party should continue to lead: "Whether the Communist Party leads is not for us to say, but for the people to say." He also cited remarks by former national leaders to support this view, such as Mao Zedong's promise after the founding of the state not to establish one-party dictatorship, and Zhao Ziyang's statement that the Communist Party could not monopolize governance.

During his testimony, Lee Cheuk-yan cited remarks by former national leaders, such as Mao Zedong's promise after the founding of the state not to establish one-party dictatorship, and Zhao Ziyang's statement that the Communist Party could not monopolize governance.

Chow Hang-tung argued that "one-party dictatorship" refers to a power structure, while "Communist Party leadership" refers to the actual power of a certain group. The two concepts are different and cannot be equated. "End one-party dictatorship" is a demand to return power to the people and end the state where the party is above the law. It does not equal "End CCP leadership," but rather equals "Building a democratic China."

The prosecution questioned whether the defendants' call for "End one-party dictatorship" meant demanding party rotation or "regime change." However, both reiterated that the position was to let the people decide whether the Communist Party should govern, and that party rotation is normal in a democratic system.

Even if "End one-party dictatorship" is equivalent to "End CCP leadership," the defence disputed that it equated to "overthrowing or destroying" the fundamental system of the state. The defence argued that "overthrow" implies violently toppling or abnormal means that drastically change the order, while "end" does not carry that connotation. For 30 years, the Alliance has been promoting human rights through persistence; merely advocating a slogan without concrete actions cannot be called "overthrow." "Destroy" carries malicious intent, but the Alliance seeks truth and exercises civil rights. Even if it harms the CCP's leadership position, it does not constitute "destruction."

The defence also questioned the claim that Communist Party leadership is the fundamental system of the state. Chow Hang-tung pointed out that the Constitution does not literally grant the Communist Party any real power; the prosecution's claim that the CCP dominates everything merely reflects political reality. The fundamental system of the state is singular—it is the socialist system, which can encompass various elements. When interpreting the Constitution, the founding principles must be considered, which cannot be derived solely from the literal text. She argued that since the court has limited itself to literal interpretation, it cannot determine whether the prosecution's interpretation is correct. If the Constitution's fundamental principle is democratic constitutionalism, then calling for an end to one-party dictatorship cannot possibly be unconstitutional.

Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan repeatedly pointed out that the prosecution never specified what actions the Alliance encouraged people to take to "End one-party dictatorship."

被告有否煽動人用「非法手段」？控方如何確立被告用「非法手段」？

The prosecution's basis is that the Alliance was not advocating constitutional amendment, but inciting people to use "illegal means" to overthrow Communist Party leadership. "Illegal means" is an important element of the charge. The defence called this the "fatal flaw" of the case, as the prosecution never specified what actions the Alliance encouraged people to take to "End one-party dictatorship."

Lee Cheuk-yan testified that he supported "End one-party dictatorship" but would not tell people to take action: "We wouldn't say 'go do things to end one-party dictatorship.'" What they called on people to do were specific actions, such as signing petitions demanding Liu Xiaobo's release or sending Christmas cards to prisoners. Chow Hang-tung also said that activities like the June 4th vigil, the Memorial Museum, and human rights advocacy have their own inherent purposes and meanings; they are the practice of the five major objectives, not incitement of others to do anything. Lee Cheuk-yan's side argued in closing that the Alliance played a supportive and educational role, and that if the Alliance had truly incited people to take concrete actions, it would have been "a real failure," because in 30 years, regardless of how many people participated in rallies and marches, nothing in Hong Kong had been carried out according to the Alliance's promotion to achieve the end of one-party dictatorship.

Chow Hang-tung further emphasized that one-party dictatorship is a power structure, not the rule of a particular party, and can only be ended through democratic and legal means. Ordinary people can only use indirect approaches—such as evidence collection and preservation, public education and empowerment, and public opinion pressure—to attempt to break the monopoly from the bottom up. She cited Albert Ho's article "How to End One-Party Dictatorship," which mentions three paths: self-reform by leaders, violent revolution, and peaceful civil resistance. The Alliance rejected violent revolution and has engaged in peaceful resistance for many years. For example, it submitted reports to the UN Human Rights Council mentioning human rights issues in the mainland and providing various recommendations to the Chinese government, all calling for the use of the rule of law and legal means to end one-party dictatorship: "We advocate that the thief should return what he stole, but we never advocated beating up the thief to take it back."

Chow Hang-tung called a housewife, Shum Lai-fong, to testify. She stated that she had participated in the June 4th candlelight vigil and the late May march as a citizen, with the purpose of mourning the dead.

The prosecution also questioned that the defendants never mentioned constitutional amendment. However, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung stated that they supported the democratic movement including constitutional amendment, and the Alliance's support for Charter 08 also reflected the expectation of legal constitutional amendment.

Regarding the prosecution's claim that the "natural and reasonable effect" of the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" was to overthrow CCP leadership, Chow Hang-tung rebutted that the natural and reasonable effect of street station activities was to call people to gatherings. It would not become an encouragement for people to do "some unknown act that is unconstitutional and ends one-party dictatorship" merely because "End one-party dictatorship" was mentioned in the process. The citizen witnesses she called also testified that they had participated in the vigils over the years to mourn the dead, not to do anything because they认同 the five major objectives. Lee Cheuk-yan's side argued that Hong Kong people "are not stupid" and it should not be assumed that their understanding of "End one-party dictatorship" must align with the prosecution's.

Regarding the prosecution's definition of "illegal means" as "unconstitutional means," Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung emphasized that the Constitution constrains the government, not the people, and they did not believe ordinary people could violate the Constitution. The defence criticized the prosecution for "circular reasoning": defining violation of Article 1 of the Constitution as illegal means, and stating that the subversive goal "End CCP leadership" violates Article 1 of the Constitution—using "unconstitutionality" to prove both the goal and the means simultaneously, which is equivalent to accusing the defendants of "violating Article 22 of the National Security Law by means of violating Article 22 of the National Security Law."

被告有否煽動顛覆意圖？

The prosecution in this case must prove "dual intent": that the defendants intended to incite others to commit subversive acts, and also intended to incite subversion. The prosecution inferred subversive intent from the defendants' alleged hostility toward the Communist Party; the defence denied this, emphasizing that the goal was to build a democratic China, not subversion.

During cross-examination, Lee Cheuk-yan agreed that he considered the CCP an authoritarian regime that suppressed the people and stifled democracy, but disagreed that he bore great hostility toward the CCP. He said, "I have no hostility in my heart, only love," stating that his criticism was based on love for the people and the hope that the Communist Party would reform so that people could obtain their due rights. He called himself "absolutely patriotic," hoping the country would be democratic, prosperous, and free, with a good future for the people. The defence emphasized that the prosecution had no evidence that Lee Cheuk-yan was "not sincere."

Chow Hang-tung reiterated that advocating "End one-party dictatorship" meant subverting the illegitimate party dictatorship, demanding accountability from those in power and "returning power to the people." She said the current charge "is like us, as the masters of the country, telling a thief to return what he stole, only to have the thief accuse us of robbery." When the judge asked whether she placed the CCP in an adversarial position, she said she would not use the word "enemy": "As Mr. Liu Xiaobo said, we have no enemies. What we resist is the system."

Chow Hang-tung stated she would not use the word "enemy" to describe the CCP, citing Liu Xiaobo: "We have no enemies. What we resist is the system."

是否明知「結束一黨專政」違法？

The prosecution alleged that after the National Security Law took effect, the defendants knowingly persisted with "End one-party dictatorship" despite its illegality; the defence denied this outright. Lee Cheuk-yan said that at the time, he "believed he was completely not breaking the law," noting that for over 30 years no one had raised issues with "End one-party dictatorship." After the National Security Law, no one or police had said the slogan violated the law or banned the Alliance's operations on national security grounds. The 2021 June 4th vigil was banned on pandemic grounds, not national security.

Chow Hang-tung acknowledged that the Alliance had discussed how to respond to the National Security Law, but believed that "fighting for democracy cannot be illegal" and that the risk "cannot be avoided." The ultimate consensus was to uphold the five major objectives. The judge pointed out that this meant they were aware of legal risks at the time, but Chow disagreed, saying she believed there was no legal violation but rather political risk, and that the National Security Law could be used as a tool for political suppression.

Chow Hang-tung acknowledged that after the implementation of the National Security Law, the Alliance had discussed how to respond, and the ultimate consensus was to uphold the five major objectives.

「結束一黨專政」是否受言論自由保障？

The prosecution argued that freedom of speech is not absolute, and that the defendants' advocacy of "End one-party dictatorship" with intent to incite the audience to subvert the regime had crossed the line of human rights protection.

Lee Cheuk-yan's side argued that Article 41 of the Chinese Constitution protects citizens' right to criticize any state organs, including the Communist Party. The Alliance never called on people to use any means, including illegal means, to end dictatorship; it merely chanted slogans and made political demands, which should be protected by freedom of speech. Chow Hang-tung also said that in a society that respects freedom of speech, advocating political reform and criticizing government actions is normal and necessary. The speech in question sought to limit and monitor power and was unpopular with the government. The court should be wary of the government escalating restrictions on speech.

During the trial, the issue was discussed as to whether the defendants' support for Liu Xiaobo and the Charter 08 he initiated, and support for people engaging in acts that might incur criminal liability in the mainland, constituted "illegal means" under the subversion charge.

煽惑人違反內地法律是否違國安法？

During their testimony, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung mentioned supporting Charter 08 initiated by Liu Xiaobo and others. The judge was concerned that the related persons had been convicted and imprisoned in the mainland, and whether the defendants supported people in committing acts that might incur criminal liability there. The judge noted that "illegal means" in the subversion charge referred to illegality in Hong Kong or the mainland, and said this should be addressed in submissions.

However, Lee Cheuk-yan's side questioned that the prosecution's basis was violation of the Constitution, and never raised "violation of domestic criminal law" as illegal means. "Illegal means" should only involve Hong Kong law. Whether the defendants incited people to use means violating mainland criminal law to promote constitutional amendment should not be an issue in this case. The prosecution also clarified that "illegal means" only targeted violation of the Chinese Constitution, not criminal law, and that the inciting act must occur in Hong Kong. The defendants must issue inciting messages in Hong Kong to a Hong Kong audience that receives them in Hong Kong. It only needs to be proven that the audience received the inciting messages; even if no incited act was carried out, the charge could be proven.
